newsitem.title: FRANCE: One-day strikes hit France in echo of 1995 unrest.
newsitem.headline: One-day strikes hit France in echo of 1995 unrest.

text.p: Tens of thousands of demonstrators marched through Paris and cities across France on Thursday as a 24-hour public employees' strike against record unemployment and government cuts hit rail, air, school and postal services.

Many schools closed, domestic and short-haul flights were drastically reduced and only one train in three was running in the first major labour unrest since a crippling public sector strike which lasted nearly four weeks in late 1995.

"All together in defence of public service, jobs and purchasing power," read the banner at the head of a giant march that sprawled through central Paris. The Communist-led CGT union said 100,000 people took part. Police had no immediate figure.
Roughly half of the country's teachers stayed away from work, as did about a third of all civil servants, postal and France Telecom staff, unions and the government said.
But the Paris bus and Metro network was operating close to normal, giving the impression of a city still ticking along, in contrast to the chaos of last year's 24-day transport strike.

Thursday's stoppage was triggered by fears among five million public employees of job cuts under Prime Minister Alain Juppe's austerity drive to cut France's deficit in time for the planned single European Union currency in 1999.
An opinion poll for the daily Le Parisien newspaper showed 64 percent of citizens sympathised with the strike.

Police, whose crowd estimates are traditionally low, said 20-25,000 people marched in Bordeaux, the southwestern city of which Juppe is mayor. Estimates for other big southern cities ranged from less than 10,000 to as many as 20,000.
Despite the big turnout, the Paris march highlighted old divisions in the labour movement over the social security reform which was one of the catalysts for last year's strike.
CGT marchers hurled abuse at Nicole Notat, whose CFDT union supported Juppe's plans to overhaul the welfare system and did not back last year's strikes.
Unions were also at odds over whether the strike presaged a repeat of the wave of labour unrest last November and December.

"There is growing anger at the grassroots which will be expressed more and more strongly because people are fed up," CGT leader Louis Viannet told Europe 1 radio. He called for a united front between public and private sector workers.
But Notat said: "I find it unpleasant and incongruous that this strike is gradually becoming a catch-all."

She told RTL radio that a simultaneous strike by doctors over health care reform was diverting the protest from its focus on the public sector. And she accused Viannet of constantly carping and failing to offer realistic alternatives.
Stoppages by air traffic controllers and staff at airlines Air France and Air Inter Europe hit flights. Air France expected to provide a third of normal flights and Air Inter one in five.

The civil servants are protesting against government plans to trim their numbers by 6,000 next year. Teachers will bear the brunt of the austerity drive, with a loss of 2,300 permanent jobs and the layoff of around 15,000 short-term contract staff.

The strikes and demonstrations reflected widespread disenchantment with conservative President Jacques Chirac, who was elected in May 1995 promising to make unemployment his top priority, cut taxes and allow higher wages.

Unemployment has since climbed to a record 12.6 percent and is still rising, taxes have gone up and purchasing power has stagnated. Chirac changed his tune a year ago, saying that cutting the deficit was France's top priority.
